agent_configs.stance_rationale: Maya Chen expressed support for the bike-lane pilot conditional on protected intersections.
Leo Martin opposes the bike-lane pilot in its current form due to concerns about losing short-stay parking.

initial_posts.content: I cycle past Main Street every day and the current layout makes intersections feel unsafe. I can support the eight-week protected bike-lane pilot only if the intersections get clear protection, not just paint. Eight weeks of data is reasonable as long as the city reports what it measures.

Losing the parking lane worries me because short-stay visitors do stop in to browse. I am not opposed in principle, but I will judge the pilot on whether the two signed loading bays actually keep deliveries on time and whether any customer visit measurement is shared transparently. Trial with measurement, not trial by default.

I am focused on what stays the same for people with limited mobility: accessible pickup spaces and an unobstructed pedestrian path. A bike lane is fine, but it cannot come at the cost of curb cuts, clear footpaths or accessible loading. I want those guarantees named before the pilot starts, not after complaints are counted.

To be clear on scope: the Cedarbrook pilot is an eight-week, reversible test on Main Street. Before any permanence decision, the city will publish counts of cyclists, deliveries, customer visits and accessibility complaints. No survey, no crash figures, and no revenue figures are being claimed at this stage. The purpose of the pilot is to generate those numbers.

scheduled_events.title: Pilot scope clarified as reversible eight-week test
scheduled_events.content: Daniel Brooks posts a short note restating that the Cedarbrook Main Street bike-lane pilot is reversible, lasts eight weeks, and that no permanence decision has been made. He lists the four metrics that will be published at the end: cyclist counts, delivery counts, customer visits, and accessibility complaints. No other figures are cited.
scheduled_events.expected_effect: Lowers base-case probability of a permanence debate erupting in round 1; raises probability of discussion staying focused on measurement definitions and pilot conditions.

scheduled_events.title: Shop owner raises loading-bay reliability question
scheduled_events.content: Leo Martin replies asking how the two signed loading bays will be enforced during morning delivery windows and whether blockage will be reported in the pilot metrics. He does not cite revenue figures but ties his conditional support to loading reliability being visible in the published counts.
scheduled_events.expected_effect: Shifts discussion toward the operational detail of the pilot; slightly raises the upside-case probability (written loading commitments) and reduces the chance the discussion defaults to a binary for/against framing.

scheduled_events.title: Resident links intersection design to safety priority
scheduled_events.content: Maya Chen reiterates that she avoids Main Street today because intersections feel unsafe, and asks whether the pilot design includes protected corners or only a lane-level buffer. She frames her support as contingent on intersection treatment, not on lane mileage.
scheduled_events.expected_effect: Keeps safety prominent as a base-case condition; raises probability that the simulated discussion converges on intersection design as a stated pilot parameter rather than an afterthought.

scheduled_events.title: Accessibility resident sets preconditions on curb access
scheduled_events.content: Priya Shah responds that accessible pickup spaces and a clear pedestrian path must be guaranteed before the pilot starts, and that accessibility complaints alone being 'counted' is not sufficient. She does not claim a specific number of complaints; she asks for design-level commitments.
scheduled_events.expected_effect: Raises downside-case probability if preconditions are left vague; increases upside-case probability that the simulated agreement includes named accessibility commitments alongside the four metrics.
